newsitem.title: CONGO: Congo pleads for French military intervention.
newsitem.headline: Congo pleads for French military intervention.

text.p: Congo pleaded for immediate French military help against armed rebels who said on Friday they had won the battle for Brazzaville airport, a claim rejected by the government.

"If France does not act as rapidly as possible, Congo's democratic regime will live or perish in bloodshed," the central African country's ambassador Pierre-Michel Nguimbi told French parliamentarians in a letter released to the press.
Denis Sassou Nguesso, who led a one-party People's Republic of Congo for 13 years until free elections in 1992, has used his private army to fight government forces since early June.
He launched a vicious assault on the capital's Maya-Maya airport on Wednesday and claimed victory on Friday.
Heavy artillery thundered for a third day, less intensely than before but picking up somewhat as night fell.
"Our partisan forces are in full control of Maya-Maya. It is now safe to land, but the runway has been damaged and would be a bit hard to negotiate," a Sassou spokesman told Reuters.
A pilot in Kinshasa who radioed Maya-Maya control tower quoted officials as saying the whole airport was controlled by Sassou. But President Pascal Lissouba's office denied it.

"Government forces are going from strength to strength. Sassou's militia is in disarray, they are totally defeated. Without a shadow of a doubt we have 100 percent control of the airport," a spokesman said by telephone from the presidency.
In the divided city centre, fighting intensified near the French embassy where ambassador Raymond Cesaire and some 30 other French nationals, including gendarmes, were trapped.
Mortars crashed into the streets around as soldiers from what is left of the fragmented national army looted any remaining goods.
France withdrew 1,250 soldiers from Brazzaville a week ago, has ordered a review of military ties to old African colonies and has declined to join a proposed U.N. peacekeeping force for Congo.
Chances look slim that it would agree to help Lissouba, whose own men assaulted Cesaire and his bodyguard on Wednesday.
"Congo, with whom France has maintained a long relationship due to history and 40-year-old policy of cooperation, is despairing to see a friend abandon it," Congo's ambassador Nguimbi wrote in Paris.

French embassy officials in Brazzaville said Congo's security minister cancelled a meeting with Cesaire, saying Sassou followers had assassinated two sub-prefects in northern towns and Lissouba had called a crisis cabinet meeting.

Some 16 people died in northern clashes just before the civil war erupted on June 5 when Lissouba tried to disarm Sassou. The fighting has otherwise been confined to the former French colonial capital of a million people.
The clashes, dampened for a week by a ceasefire before they resumed this week, have killed some 1,000 to 3,000 residents and sent thousands more fleeing to the outskirts for safety.
Many sought refuge in southern Brazzaville, held by the neutral city mayor Bernard Kolelas, but shelling has caused damage there as well.
Lissouba holds a central part and Sassou the north of the city that hugs the bank of the Congo river, facing Kinshasa, capital of what was the Belgian Congo.
The three men were to have fought now unlikely presidential elections due exactly a month on Friday. Sassou says Lissouba is incapable of organising them fairly.
The International Committee of the Red Cross, the last aid agency at work in Brazzaville, withdrew its last four foreign staff on Thursday.
The remains of people killed by the fighting -- most of them civilians -- lie decomposing in the no man's lands. Some have lain there in the tropical heat for three weeks.
